task.goal: Improve access to a one-day neighborhood workshop in a temporary hall with uneven entrances.
hard_constraints: Three volunteers, one week, removable signs and portable chairs; no structural alterations.
Do not advertise an entrance as accessible until its route is checked.
Measure arrival success, waiting and dignified participation including seated options.
task.available_resources: Hall plan and a pre-event route inspection.
task.expected_result: An accessible arrival and activity layout.

DIRECT_FULL.title: One checked arrival route and a seated activity loop
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make one verified route the organizing spine of the workshop: entrance, welcome point, activities and exit. The mechanism is reducing route uncertainty and unnecessary movement, while making seated participation part of every activity.

During the week, two volunteers use the hall plan and inspect the actual approach, thresholds, doors, surfaces, circulation space, toilets and exit arrangements. Record barriers and unresolved questions; a visual inspection alone cannot establish suitability for every person. Select the most usable entrance only after checking its complete route. Describe verified conditions rather than promising universal accessibility. If no usable route exists, signs and chairs cannot solve that limitation; the proposed indoor arrangement is not viable for people excluded by those barriers.

Place removable direction signs at decision points and portable chairs at welcome, waiting and activity positions without narrowing circulation or escape routes. Arrange activities in a short loop, with a seated version offering the same task and interaction as standing participation. Avoid making seated participants request a separate demonstration.

On the day, one volunteer welcomes arrivals, one supports circulation and waiting, and one facilitates activities. This assumes workshop content can be delivered by one facilitator, with the others helping when arrival demand falls. Required resources are the plan, inspection time, signs and chairs. The main limits are an unsuitable entrance, inaccessible essential facilities, or activities that cannot provide equivalent seated participation.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Before opening, compare this layout with a simple main-door-and-standing-stations sketch. Walk both routes from the approach and trace seated participation through each activity. Reject the proposal if it retains an unchecked barrier, obstructs an exit or requires extra help merely to participate seated. During the event, tally attempted and successful arrivals, wrong turns, arrival-to-participation waiting times and abandonment. Ask participants privately whether they could join their preferred activities, remain seated when wanted and receive help without feeling singled out. A shorter route alone is not evidence of dignified participation.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Bring the whole workshop to a checked arrival area
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Keep participants in one shared, seated-capable activity area near a checked entrance, and rotate the workshop content to them. The mechanism is removing repeated travel between stations rather than improving navigation around the entire hall.

Use the plan and pre-event inspection to identify an area reached by a usable entrance route, with sufficient circulation, safe exit access and a checked route to essential facilities. Do not call the entrance accessible before inspection. Explain any remaining barriers accurately. If no suitable area and route exist, this alternative cannot provide the intended access within the available resources.

Arrange portable chairs in an open group layout, leaving spaces that let people using mobility devices sit alongside companions rather than at a separate edge. Standing participation remains optional. Deliver activities sequentially to the group, moving explanations and any existing workshop materials between participants instead of asking participants to circulate. Use removable signs to direct arrivals to this single destination.

During preparation, adapt each activity so its central experience works from a seated position. One volunteer handles arrival and waiting, one leads the activity, and one circulates to repeat explanations, support participation and keep routes clear. This assumes the workshop can use shared demonstrations, discussion or portable tasks. It is less suitable for activities tied to fixed equipment elsewhere in the hall, and a single group may limit throughput or create noise. Late arrivals need a brief orientation that does not interrupt everyone else.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Prototype one representative activity in the proposed seating arrangement and compare it with a conventional move-between-stations version. Use an ordinary chair to check seated reach and visibility, while recognizing this does not simulate every disability. Reject or revise the design if seated participants cannot perform the core task, see the demonstration or interact comparably. On the day, record arrival success, waiting until the next usable activity and any departures caused by waiting. Ask whether people could participate with companions, choose their posture and avoid unwanted public assistance. Check that reduced movement has not produced longer exclusionary waits.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Paced arrivals with optional personal wayfinding
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use optional arrival windows and a volunteer greeting service to reduce simultaneous demand at a checked entrance. The mechanism is matching assistance capacity to arrivals, so people encounter less congestion and can obtain directions without navigating alone.

Inspect the approach, entrances, internal route, essential facilities and exits during the week. Choose a route only on the evidence of that inspection and communicate its actual conditions. Personal assistance cannot make an impassable threshold accessible: do not plan lifting, carrying or improvised physical transfers. If no suitable route exists, this approach cannot remedy the access failure.

Offer staggered arrival windows through whatever workshop communication already exists, while retaining walk-in participation. Explain that greeting assistance is optional and available to anyone; do not require disability disclosure. If advance contact is unavailable, the greeting service still operates, but the benefit from pacing is uncertain.

Place removable signs to the verified welcome point and portable waiting chairs clear of circulation. One volunteer greets arrivals and records demand; a second offers directions or accompaniment with consent; the third runs a seated-capable opening activity that people can join as they arrive. Keep the main activity layout compact, with equivalent seated options throughout. Never hold someone outside solely because their arrival window has not begun.

This assumes arrival demand can be spread and the workshop can accommodate a rolling start. It is vulnerable to clustered walk-ins, a long accompaniment route or facilitation that needs all three volunteers.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Run a short rehearsal with volunteers alternating as arrivals: compare clustered arrivals with the same number spread across windows. Record time to greeting, time to activity and occasions when accompaniment leaves welcome unattended. Treat this as a capacity check, not proof of accessibility. Reject the staffing arrangement if a plausible small cluster causes unmanageable waiting. During the event, count successful and unsuccessful arrivals, assistance requests, waiting times and abandonment. Ask whether assistance felt optional and respectful and whether seated participants joined equivalent activities. Compare waits for scheduled arrivals and walk-ins to detect unfair displacement.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Duplicate the complete workshop across independently reachable zones
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Create two small workshop zones, each offering the complete program, when different checked entrances reach usable parts of the hall but an internal barrier makes a shared layout difficult. The mechanism is duplicating access to the workshop itself: participants need not cross the problematic connection to obtain the full experience. This differs from directing everyone along one preferred route or rotating content around one shared group.

Use the hall plan and pre-event inspection to check both approach routes, entrances, zone circulation, essential facilities and exits. Advertise only verified route conditions after inspection. Proceed only if both zones independently support safe arrival and participation; duplication cannot compensate for an unusable entrance or missing essential facilities.

During the week, prepare the same short activity sequence for both zones. Use portable chairs to provide seated participation, companion seating and room for mobility devices within each group. Removable signs explain which checked entrance serves each zone and state that both offer the full workshop. Let participants choose their group without disability disclosure, and keep companions together.

On the day, one volunteer facilitates each zone while the third circulates between welcome points, checks waiting and helps with orientation by consent. Each facilitator must be able to welcome arrivals briefly without leaving the group unsupported. Both zones need comparable visibility, interaction and seated access to every core task.

This requires a workshop that two volunteers can each deliver using existing resources, without scarce equipment that cannot be shared. It may reduce group size and require repeated explanations. It also divides the social gathering; if a single whole-group experience is essential, this alternative is unsuitable.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare the two-zone plan with a single shared workshop location. Trace each arrival route and rehearse one complete activity in each zone, including a simultaneous arrival at both entrances. Reject duplication if either group loses a core task, needs to cross the barrier, or cannot be welcomed adequately. During the event, tally attempted and successful arrivals by entrance, arrival-to-activity waiting, abandonment and missed activities. Privately ask whether participants could stay with companions, choose seated participation and receive equivalent attention without feeling segregated. These checks can expose failures; a small rehearsal cannot establish suitability for every participant.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Let participants choose between routes with different barriers
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Provide a factual route menu so participants can select the entrance that fits their needs. The mechanism is matching people to different verified route conditions: the shortest approach may involve steps, while another may avoid steps but require a longer journey or a heavier door. This could improve arrival success when no entrance is best for everyone.

During the week, two volunteers use the hall plan and pre-event inspection to check each potentially useful approach through to the same workshop area, including essential facilities and exits. Record observable conditions such as steps, thresholds, surface changes, door operation and resting opportunities. Distinguish estimates from measurements and leave uncertain features explicitly unresolved. Do not advertise any entrance as accessible before checking its route.

Proceed only if at least two usable routes offer meaningfully different advantages and both reach the shared activity area. Prepare removable signs presenting those differences at an upstream decision point, before visitors commit to an entrance. Use plain descriptions rather than disability categories or a universal accessibility label. Participants choose without disclosing a condition; a volunteer can explain the options without assigning a route.

Place portable resting chairs where inspection identifies safe space, keeping circulation and exits clear. In the shared workshop, provide integrated seating and make every core activity available seated. One volunteer welcomes and explains route choices, one supports the activity, and one facilitates.

This needs only the plan, inspection, signs and chairs, but assumes visitors can reach a common decision point and the activity works with two volunteers. It cannot overcome an impassable entrance, and it offers little benefit if all approaches share the same barrier. An unsuitable approach must remain clearly excluded from the offered choices.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare the route-menu sketch with signs directing everyone to the single most usable entrance. Have volunteers trace both plans against contrasting needs, such as avoiding steps versus minimizing walking. Reject the menu if it offers no useful alternative, places information after a difficult commitment, or directs anyone onto an unchecked segment. This is an inspection exercise, not evidence of suitability for every disability. During the event, tally attempted and successful arrivals, route reversals, arrival-to-activity waiting and abandonment. Privately ask whether route information supported a useful choice, help felt respectful, and participants could join the core activities seated with companions. If choice increases confusion without improving arrival success, simplify the directions.

EXPAND.title: Separate quiet participation from noisy activity
EXPAND.proposal:
Organize the workshop by sound and attention demands. The mechanism is reducing interference between activities so participants can hear explanations, follow conversation and choose a less stimulating place without leaving the workshop. This addresses participation barriers that a shorter arrival route alone does not resolve.

Use the hall plan and pre-event inspection to identify a quiet activity area away from entrance conversations and any noisy workshop tasks. Check the complete approach, entrance, internal connections, essential facilities and exits before describing access conditions. Do not advertise an entrance as accessible before checking its route. If an unavoidable physical barrier prevents entry, this arrangement cannot remedy it.

Arrange portable chairs so participants can see one another and the facilitator, with companion spaces and clear circulation. Put noisy tasks at the greatest practical distance from discussion. Use removable signs to identify the areas and explain that either is open to everyone. Provide the same core task and seated options in both areas where existing workshop materials permit; avoid assigning disabled participants to a separate group.

One volunteer welcomes arrivals, one facilitates the main activity and one supports the quiet area. During the week, rehearse the same short explanation in both locations and prepare equivalent instructions. This assumes the room provides useful acoustic separation and the workshop can run with two facilitators. Without partitions, distance may provide little benefit; duplicating facilitation may also reduce capacity. The resources are the plan, inspection, chairs, signs and existing workshop materials.
EXPAND.experiment: Before opening, compare the proposed zones with an undivided layout while volunteers produce ordinary entrance conversation and deliver a representative explanation. Check whether a seated listener can follow the explanation without repeated clarification. Revise or reject the zoning if it provides no useful improvement or compromises routes. On the day, tally attempted and successful arrivals, time until participation, and departures before joining. Ask privately whether participants could hear, choose a suitable area, participate seated and stay with companions without feeling segregated. Acoustic benefit remains uncertain until checked under actual attendance.

EXPAND.title: Make instructions available without waiting for a volunteer
EXPAND.proposal:
Use removable signs as persistent, plain-language activity instructions as well as directions. The mechanism is removing dependence on catching a spoken briefing or securing individual volunteer attention. Participants can inspect the next step, start when ready and revisit instructions without publicly requesting repetition.

Inspect the full arrival route, activity positions, essential facilities and exits using the hall plan. Describe only verified conditions, and do not advertise an entrance as accessible before its route is checked. Signs cannot compensate for an impassable entrance or an unsuitable activity.

For each activity, prepare a short sign stating its purpose, first action, subsequent steps and how to obtain help. Use large, legible text, simple symbols accompanied by words, and an explicit seated method offering the same core experience. Place instructions where standing and seated participants can read them without entering circulation space. Use chairs at activity positions and provide spaces alongside them for participants using mobility devices.

One volunteer welcomes arrivals, one demonstrates or explains instructions when requested, and one supports activities and monitors waiting. Spoken explanation remains available: text and symbols will not serve everyone, including some people with visual, reading or cognitive access needs. No diagnosis or explanation should be required to request help.

Preparation fits within the week if activities have a small number of stable steps. It requires only the existing workshop content, removable signs, chairs, plan and inspection. Its main limits are complex tasks, inaccessible sign placement and activities requiring continuous supervision; written instructions must never replace necessary safety oversight.
EXPAND.experiment: Prepare one activity sign and compare a sign-supported start with a spoken-briefing-only start. Have volunteers take turns approaching without an introduction; check whether they can identify and perform the first safe step from a seated position. This is a usability inspection, not evidence that all participants can use the signs. Reject or simplify instructions that cause consequential misunderstandings. During the event, record arrival successes and failures, waiting until meaningful participation and requests for clarification. Ask privately whether participants could choose seated participation and obtain explanations respectfully. Shorter waits count as improvement only if understanding and participation are preserved.

EXPAND.title: Remove opposing traffic at a verified bottleneck
EXPAND.proposal:
Where inspection finds that people entering and leaving repeatedly obstruct one another, organize movement to prevent opposing flows at that specific location. The mechanism is reducing encounters that force people to reverse, squeeze past others or surrender their place. This differs from spreading arrival times: participants may arrive whenever they wish, while the internal movement pattern reduces conflict.

Use the hall plan and inspection to identify whether a genuine bottleneck exists. Check approaches, thresholds, doors, turning space, essential facilities and emergency arrangements. A separate normal departure route is useful only if its full route is checked and suitable for the people using it. Do not advertise any entrance as accessible before checking its route.

If the hall supports it, use removable arrows to direct ordinary entry and departure along separate paths around the activity area. Keep emergency exits and required circulation clear. If only one suitable passage exists, a volunteer can offer brief, consent-based coordination of opposing movement, with waiting chairs outside the passage. Never turn a voluntary circulation pattern into a restriction on emergency escape or access to essential facilities.

One volunteer welcomes arrivals, one monitors the bottleneck during busy periods, and one facilitates seated-capable activities. Place chairs so participants can join the core activity without repeatedly crossing the bottleneck. Preparation requires the plan, inspection, signs and chairs, with no alterations.

This alternative is useful only when opposing movement is a material problem. It may fail if the route is intrinsically impassable, the alternative path adds excessive travel, or monitoring consumes more volunteer capacity than it saves. It should be dropped if inspection finds no meaningful traffic conflict.
EXPAND.experiment: Before opening, compare ordinary two-way movement with the proposed pattern using volunteers entering, leaving and waiting in turn. Inspect passing and turning space; an ordinary chair does not simulate a mobility device. Reject the arrangement if it creates a new obstruction, increases required travel substantially or depends on preventing essential movement. During the event, tally attempted and successful arrivals, bottleneck waits, time to participation and occasions when someone must retreat. Ask privately whether participants could move and participate seated without pressure, unwanted assistance or being made to feel responsible for delays.

EXPAND.title: Preserve people’s turns without requiring a standing queue
EXPAND.proposal:
Replace any physical queue for welcome or activity turns with a volunteer-managed order that does not depend on where someone stands or sits. The mechanism is separating access to a turn from the ability to remain in line. Participants can rest, stay beside companions or use a seated activity position without losing their place.

During the week, use the hall plan and route inspection to check the approach, entrance, waiting area, activity positions, essential facilities and exits. Do not advertise an entrance as accessible before its route is checked. Describe verified conditions and remaining barriers. If no usable entrance route exists, this arrangement cannot resolve that exclusion.

Use portable chairs to create a shared waiting area beside the activity, leaving circulation, turning space and exits clear. Include spaces for mobility devices among the chairs. Removable signs explain that participants retain their turn wherever they wait in the designated area and can request a discreet personal notification. Nobody must disclose a disability or accept a chair.

One volunteer welcomes arrivals and maintains their order; a second notifies the next participant and supports movement with consent; the third facilitates. At each activity, provide an equivalent seated method as a normal choice. Participants who need more time to reach the activity keep their turn. Avoid calling out disability information or requiring participants to respond to an audible announcement.

This assumes that waiting for individual turns is a meaningful barrier and that one facilitator can run the workshop. It requires only the plan, inspection, signs and chairs. A small queue can be tracked by the welcome volunteer; demand exceeding reliable tracking capacity is a practical limit. Removing standing does not itself shorten service time, and the approach adds little if activities have no queues.
EXPAND.experiment: After checking the route, have the three volunteers rehearse arrival, waiting and a seated activity turn, alternating roles. Compare an ordinary standing line with the proposed arrangement using the same sequence and service duration. Record successful arrivals at the activity, waiting time, required standing, lost turns and whether a seated participant receives the same task and interaction. Include someone waiting away from the next activity position and someone who misses a spoken notification. Reject or simplify the arrangement if order becomes unreliable, notification requires public disclosure, circulation is obstructed or waiting grows materially. On the day, tally arrival attempts and completions without recording identities, sample waiting times, and ask participants whether they could rest, retain their turn and participate in their preferred position. Volunteer rehearsal cannot establish suitability for every participant.
